# The genetic architecture of the load linked to dominant and recessive self-incompatibility alleles in Arabidopsis halleri and Arabidopsis lyrata ## Authors - Audrey Le Veve1 ([ORCID: 0000-0001-5895-370X](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5895-370X)) - Mathieu Genete1 - Christelle Lepers-Blassiau1 - Chloé Ponitzki1 - Céline Poux1 - Xavier Vekemans1 - Eleonore Durand1 - Vincent Castric1 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-4461-4915](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4461-4915)) † ### Affiliations 1. Univ. Lille, CNRS, UMR 8198 – Evo-Eco-Paleo Lille France ([ROR:02kzqn938](https://ror.org/02kzqn938)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract The long-term balancing selection acting on mating types or sex-determining genes is expected to lead to the accumulation of deleterious mutations in the tightly linked chromosomal segments that are locally ‘sheltered’ from purifying selection. However, the factors determining the extent of this accumulation are poorly understood. Here, we took advantage of variations in the intensity of balancing selection along a dominance hierarchy formed by alleles at the sporophytic self-incompatibility system of the Brassicaceae to compare the pace at which linked deleterious mutations accumulate among them. We first experimentally measured the phenotypic manifestation of the linked load at three different levels of the dominance hierarchy. We then sequenced and phased polymorphisms in the chromosomal regions linked to 126 distinct copies of S-alleles in two populations of Arabidopsis halleri and three populations of Arabidopsis lyrata. We find that linkage to the S-locus locally distorts phylogenies over about 10–30 kb along the chromosome. The more intense balancing selection on dominant S-alleles results in greater fixation of linked deleterious mutations, while recessive S-alleles accumulate more linked deleterious mutations that are segregating. Hence, the structure rather than the overall magnitude of the linked genetic load differs between dominant and recessive S-alleles. Our results have consequences for the long-term evolution of new S-alleles, the evolution of dominance modifiers between them, and raise the question of why the non-recombining regions of some sex and mating type chromosomes expand over evolutionary times while others, such as the S-locus of the Brassicaceae, remain restricted to small chromosomal regions. ## Introduction The existence of sexes or mating types leads to one of the strongest forms of long-term balancing selection and is often associated with clusters of polymorphisms around sex/mating-type-controlling regions kept together by structural rearrangements. In some cases, such rearrangements can span almost entire chromosomes, for example, sex chromosomes in mammals (Katsura et al., 2012) or mating-type chromosomes in ascomycete fungi (Hartmann et al., 2021), while in others they remain limited to relatively small genomic regions, for example, chromosomal inversions controlling male reproductive morphs in the ruff (Lamichhaney et al., 2016), mating-type loci in some basidiomycete fungi, segregating indels controlling pin vs. thrum floral morphs in Primula (Cocker et al., 2018). The long-term balancing selection acting on these systems is expected to lead to the accumulation of deleterious mutations in the tightly linked chromosomal segments that are ‘sheltered’ from purifying selection by the presence of the balanced polymorphism (Uyenoyama, 1997; Uyenoyama, 2005). These deleterious mutations can have drastic short- and long-term consequences for the evolution of the species, and determining the processes by which they accumulate is crucial to understand how the rearranged regions can either expand along the chromosomes or conversely remain restricted to limited genomic tracts (Jay et al., 2021; Jay et al., 2022). Self-incompatibility (SI) is a genetic mechanism allowing recognition and rejection of self-pollen by hermaphrodite individuals, thereby preventing inbreeding and promoting outcrossing in hermaphroditic plant species (Nettancourt, 2001). In the Brassicaceae family, SI is controlled by a single non-recombining chromosomal region, the S-locus (Schopfer et al., 1999; Kusaba et al., 2001). SI is one of the most prominent examples of long-term balancing selection (Uyenoyama, 2003), and as such deleterious mutations are expected to accumulate in very close genetic linkage to the S-alleles because of the indirect effects of linked selection (Uyenoyama, 2005). Population genetics models predict that recessive deleterious variants should accumulate within specific S-allele lineages (Uyenoyama, 2003; Llaurens et al., 2009b) and should then be reshuffled among them by recombination. However, due to the technical difficulty of phasing polymorphisms, this process has rarely been characterised in detail (Castric and Vekemans, 2004). A key feature of sporophytic SI systems, also shared by sex chromosomes, is the existence of dominance interactions between S-alleles. While most individuals are heterozygous at the S-locus and thus carry two different S-alleles, only one of them is generally expressed at the phenotypic level. This is especially true for the pollen specificity, where S-alleles follow a complex genetic dominance hierarchy (Llaurens et al., 2008; Durand et al., 2014). In Arabidopsis lyrata and Arabidopsis halleri, the S-alleles are distributed into four classes of dominance, with increasing dominance from class I to class IV and linear dominance also observed inside some of the classes. Similar patterns of dominance between S-alleles occur in Brassica species, but with only two classes (Hatakeyama et al., 1998; Kakizaki et al., 2003; Yasuda et al., 2017). This system is genetically determined and controlled by small RNAs molecules produced by dominant S-alleles that are able to target and repress expression of the recessive S-alleles in pollen (Durand et al., 2014; Yasuda et al., 2017). The evolutionary properties of S-alleles are expected to vary in a predictable manner along the dominance hierarchy because balancing selection acts more strongly on dominant than on recessive S-alleles as the latter are often masked at the phenotypic level (Billiard et al., 2007). As a result, the dynamics of accumulation of deleterious variation may differ in close linkage with dominant vs. recessive S-alleles. Specifically, recessive S-alleles can form homozygous combinations in natural populations more often than dominant S-alleles (Billiard et al., 2007), such that recombination can occur occasionally between distinct gene copies of the same recessive S-allele, providing the opportunity for the linked recessive deleterious mutations to be purged from within the S-locus itself. In addition, because recessive S-alleles reach higher population frequencies (Billiard et al., 2007; Llaurens et al., 2008), purifying selection on linked deleterious variants is expected to have higher efficacy among gene copies of recessive than dominant S-alleles. This is expected to result in a higher fixation probability of deleterious variants linked to the class of dominant S-alleles than to the class of recessive S-alleles (Llaurens et al., 2009b). Thus, the level of dominance of S-alleles determines the intensity of purifying selection acting upon them. This situation closely resembles that of the differential evolution of sex chromosomes, where Y chromosomes (similar to dominant S-alleles) tend to accumulate more deleterious variation than X chromosomes (similar to recessive S-alleles; Llaurens et al., 2009b; Goubet et al., 2012). Empirical support for this simple prediction has been conflicting, though. Based on phenotypic measurements in A. halleri, Llaurens et al., 2009b observed a decrease of fitness associated by enforced homozygosity for one of the most dominant S-alleles (Ah15) but not for the most recessive S-allele of the allelic series (Ah01). In contrast, Stift et al., 2013 observed no effect of dominance on the genetic load linked to three dominant vs. recessive S-alleles in a natural population of the closely related A. lyrata. Hence, the data available so far are inconclusive, but are restricted to very small numbers of S-alleles. They are also based on inherently limited phenotypic measurements, seriously limiting the power of the comparisons, and preventing proper generalisation of the effect of the intensity of balancing selection on the accumulation of linked deleterious variation. In this study, we combined phenotypic, genomic, and theoretical approaches to finely dissect the patterns of accumulation of deleterious variation linked to the S-locus supergene in A. halleri and A. lyrata, depending on dominance levels of S-allele. We first extended the phenotypic approach of Llaurens et al., 2009b to a series of additional S-alleles from the same local A. halleri population to evaluate the effect of S-allele dominance on the sheltered load. We then used parent–offspring trios and targeted genome re-sequencing to directly quantify the accumulation of putative deleterious mutations linked to phased dominant vs. recessive S-alleles in two A. halleri and three A. lyrata natural populations. Finally, we used stochastic simulations to refine the theoretical predictions about the patterns of accumulation of recessive deleterious mutations linked to dominant vs. recessive S-alleles. Overall, our results provide a more nuanced view of the effect of the intensity of balancing selection on the sheltered load, in which the structure of the sheltered load rather than its magnitude differs among S-alleles from different dominance classes. ## Results ### The genetic load linked to the S-locus varies among S-alleles, but is not correlated with dominance We first expanded the experimental approach of Llaurens et al., 2009b to phenotypically evaluate the effect of S-allele dominance on the intensity of the sheltered load. The previous study focused on three S-alleles (Ah01, Ah02, and Ah15; Llaurens et al., 2009b). Here we included two S-alleles from the same local population (Nivelle, France): Ah03 and Ah04, and included Ah01 again for comparative purposes. In the Arabidopsis genus, S-alleles have been shown to form a complex dominance hierarchy (Llaurens et al., 2008; Durand et al., 2014). This hierarchy is largely associated with the phylogeny of S-alleles (Durand et al., 2014), and at least four phylogenetic classes (I, II, III, and IV) have been described, from the most recessive (class I) to the most dominant of S-alleles (class IV). Dominance interactions also exist among S-alleles within classes, such that these five S-alleles form the following dominance hierarchy (Llaurens et al., 2008; Durand et al., 2014): Ah01Ahx, on pistils of a AhxAhz plant where z≠y, or on a AhxAhx pistil when available; Supplementary file 1a). We obtained 399 offspring from a total of six such crosses. Note that our experimental procedure differs slightly from that of Llaurens et al., 2009b in that their procedure required a CO2 treatment to bypass the SI system and obtain selfed offspring, while here we took advantage of the dominance interactions to obtain outcrossed S-locus homozygous individuals that we phenotypically compared to their full-sibs with S-locus heterozygous genotypes. Note also that the S-locus homozygous offspring we obtained contain distinct gene copies of a given S-allele lineage. Hence, they could in principle carry distinct suites of linked deleterious mutations in case these mutations segregate within S-allele lineages. We first tested whether homozygosity at the S-locus affected survival by measuring for each cross the proportion of homozygotes at the S-locus reaching the reproductive stage for three S-alleles (in two replicate families per S-allele; Supplementary file 1a). The proportion of Ah01/Ah01 and Ah04/Ah04 homozygotes surviving to the reproductive stage was consistent with Mendelian expectations in their respective families. However, we observed a significant decrease of Ah03/Ah03 homozygotes at the reproductive stage compared with Mendelian expectations (Supplementary file 1a), whereas the observed proportion of the Ah03 S-allele among heterozygous individuals did not depart from expectations (2/3 = 0.67; Table 1). Thus, the increased mortality is associated with Ah03 homozygosity, rather than with a lower performance of individuals carrying the Ah03 S-allele itself. Overall, a genetic load was thus observed linked to the Ah03 S-alleles, which is at an intermediate level of dominance, but neither to the most dominant (Ah04) nor to the most recessive (Ah01) S-allele. We first used permutations to test whether the mean trait value of homozygotes differed from that in heterozygotes. Overall, with a single exception, we found no effect of homozygosity at the S-locus on variation of the traits measured (Figure 1; Supplementary file 1b). The maximum length of flowering stems was the exception to this general pattern, with longer reproductive stems for S-locus homozygous than heterozygous genotypes, hence in the opposite direction from our expectation of lower fitness in homozygotes. For this trait, there was significant variation among replicate families for homozygotes of the recessive allele Ah01 but not of the dominant allele Ah04 (Supplementary file 1c). We then used generalised linear models (GLM) to evaluate the effect of dominance (considered as a continuous variable with fixed effect) on the mean phenotypic value of homozygotes compared to heterozygotes for each trait (Supplementary file 1d; treating family of origin, attacks by phytopathogens, phytophagous and oxidative stress as random effects whenever necessary). We also observed no effect of S-allele dominance on the contrast between S-locus homozygotes and heterozygotes for any of these traits. A single of the 13 traits was an exception to this general pattern, but again the effect was in the opposite direction from our expectation, with an earlier rather than delayed appearance of the first leaf for homozygotes of more dominant S-alleles (Supplementary file 1d). Overall, our phenotypic results confirmed the presence of a detectable linked load on some phenotypic traits (survival; time to produce the first leaf), but we could not replicate the observation of Llaurens et al., 2009b that dominant S-alleles carry a more severe deleterious load than recessive S-alleles, even though our samples were obtained from the same local population. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/94972/elife-94972-fig1-v1.jpg) **Figure 1.:** For each trait, the phenotypic values in homozygotes (in grey; n=72) were normalised relative to the mean phenotypic values in heterozygotes (in black; n=86). We combined a parent–offspring trio approach with sequencing of the S-locus flanking regions to phase the mutations segregating in the S-locus flanking regions with their respective S-alleles. Briefly, we used a previously developed sequence capture protocol specifically targeting the nucleotide sequences over 75 kb on each side of the S-locus along with a series of 100 control regions from throughout the genome (Le Veve et al., 2023), and analysed nucleotide sequence polymorphism (including only invariant and biallelic SNPs), based on the A. lyrata reference genome (Hu et al., 2011). We define a haplotype as a unique combination of mutations along the phased chromosome, and an S-allele lineage as the collection of gene copies of a given functional S-allele (different functional S-alleles are distinguished based on their strong sequence divergence at the S-locus pollen and pistil genes). Different gene copies within an S-allele lineage can thus be associated with distinct linked haplotypes in the flanking regions. The S-alleles were identified based on short reads sequences according to a previously published method (Genete et al., 2020). We analysed two closely related A. halleri populations from Europe (Nivelle and Mortagne) and three allogamous A. lyrata populations from North America (IND, PIN, and TSS; Foxe et al., 2010). Overall, we were able to reconstruct 34 haplotypes linked to a total of 12 distinct S-allele lineages in Nivelle, 38 haplotypes linked to 11 distinct S-allele lineages in Mortagne, and 16, 22, and 16 haplotypes associated with 6, 7, and 5 distinct S-allele lineages in populations IND, PIN, and TSS, respectively (Supplementary file 1e). Nine of the S-alleles were shared between the two A. halleri populations (Ah01, Ah03, Ah04, Ah05, Ah12, Ah20, Ah24, Ah25, and Ah59). In the populations of A. lyrata, four S-alleles were shared between PIN and TSS (Ah01*, Ah03*, Ah18*, and Ah63*), five S-alleles were shared between PIN and IND (Ah01*, Ah03*, Ah46*, and Ah63*), four S-alleles were shared between IND and TSS (Ah01*, Ah03*, Ah31*, and Ah63*), and three were shared across all three (Ah01*, Ah03*, and Ah63*). Note that for convenience, we used A. halleri notations (with the addition of a *) to refer to the trans-specifically shared A. lyrata S-alleles. Altogether, we were able to obtain the phased flanking sequences of 126 S-locus haplotypes, comprising a total of 4854 variable sites. This provides considerable power to evaluate the local accumulation of linked mutations across S-alleles of different levels of dominance and examine their patterns of conservation between populations and between species. Mutations in the S-locus flanking regions can be exchanged between S-alleles by recombination and between local populations by migration (Charlesworth, 2006). The relative time scale of these two processes (recombination vs. migration) determines the distribution of the linked mutations. To capture the chromosomal extent of this effect of linkage to S-alleles, we developed a new phylogenetic method comparing the likelihood of two contrasted topologies of interest in overlapping windows along the chromosome: (1) the topology clustering haplotypes by the populations where they came from vs. (2) the topology clustering them by the S-allele to which they are linked (Figure 2A). This allowed us to evaluate the progressive shift from a predominant topology by S-alleles close to the S-locus to a topology by populations further along the chromosome and in unlinked control regions (Figure 2B). The difference in log likelihood between the two topologies decreased significantly with distance to the S-locus (Pearson coefficient = –0.015 and –0.010 for A. halleri and A. lyrata, respectively; p-values<2e-16). In A. halleri, the topology grouping haplotypes by populations became more likely than the topology grouping them by S-alleles at a distance of around 30 kb from the S-locus, but even at a distance of 50 kb the phylogenetic structure was still different from that in regions unlinked to the S-locus used as controls for the genomic background (Le Veve et al., 2023; Figure 2B). In A. lyrata, the shift was even more rapid (within 10–15 kb), although we note that the phylogenetic structure of the control regions was less resolved (Figure 2B). To evaluate these patterns more directly, we first examined the data using a major component analysis (MCA, a modified version of PCA adapted to binary data, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) and using simple phylogenetic reconstructions (Figure 2B—figure supplement 3–6). We confirmed that haplotypes linked to a given S-allele tended to cluster together in the most tightly linked region, and that this grouping by S-alleles was progressively lost in favour of a grouping by population of origin in the most distant regions. Following Kamau et al., 2007, we compared the fixation index FST among local populations and among S-alleles in A. lyrata and A. halleri. In both A. halleri and A. lyrata, FST values among S-alleles were high in regions close to the S-locus and quickly decreased to reach the background level (Figure 2B—figure supplement 8) as the distance from the S-locus increased. In parallel, the differentiation among populations followed roughly the opposite pattern, that is, it was initially low in regions close to the S-locus (as expected under strong balancing selection) and increased up to background level within the first few kilobases (Figure 2—figure supplement 7). In line with our phylogenetic analysis, differentiation between populations started to exceed differentiation between S-alleles much closer to the S-locus in the A. lyrata than in the A. halleri populations (Figure 2—figure supplements 3–5 and Figure 2—figure supplement 7B). Finally, we explored the fine-scale patterns of association within populations between individual S-alleles and SNP in the linked and the control regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 8). As expected, the vast majority of significant associations were found for the most closely linked SNPs. With a single exception, all S-alleles were associated with unique SNPs in the 50 kb region around the S-locus, albeit with substantial heterogeneity among S-alleles in the patterns and extent of associations that they show (Figure 2—figure supplement 8). Overall, our results indicate that due to limited recombination, the S-alleles carry a specific set of polymorphic sites in the linked region. This association fades away for more distant sites over a few kilobases, where population structure becomes predominant, as in the rest of the genome. The vertical lines correspond to the mean number of significantly associated SNPs in the first 25 kb (solid lines) and the 25–50 kb interval (dashed lines) away from S-locus. ### No overall evidence that dominant S-alleles accumulate more linked deleterious mutations Llaurens et al., 2009b predicted that recessive deleterious mutations should fix more readily when linked to dominant S-alleles than when linked to recessive S-alleles. To test this prediction, we investigated the correlation between the level of dominance of the S-alleles and their total number of zerofold degenerate mutations (S0f) or the ratio of zerofold to fourfold mutations (S0f/S4f) for the phased haplotypes, assuming that the vast majority of zerofold degenerate mutations are deleterious. Based on the results presented above and the results of our previous study (Le Veve et al., 2023), for the rest of our analyses we focused on the phased haplotypes over the first 25 kb on either side of the S-locus. We found no overall effect of dominance on S0f (p-values = 0.54 and 0.07 for A. halleri and A. lyrata, respectively; Figure 3; Supplementary file 1f) or S0f/S4f (p-values = 0.54 and 0.07 for A. halleri and A. lyrata, respectively; Supplementary file 1f). Extending the analysis to all non-synonymous mutations or to deleterious mutations predicted by SIFT4G and by SNPeff led to identical conclusions (Supplementary file 1f). Overall, our genomic results did not confirm the prediction that dominant S-alleles accumulate a larger number of putatively deleterious mutations in their linked regions. We note that the particular S-allele whose sheltered load was quantified in Llaurens et al., 2009b (Ah15, red arrow in Figure 3A) appears to be one of the S-alleles associated with the highest number of zerofold degenerate mutations among all S-alleles of the most dominant class (class IV). ![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/94972/elife-94972-fig3-v1.jpg) **Figure 3.:** Each dot represents the mean number of mutations observed among haplotypes linked to one S-allele in one population. Red dots correspond to the IND population, black dots to the PIN population, and blue dots to the TSS population. ### The structure of the linked genetic load differs between dominant and recessive S-alleles Theory predicts that dominant S-alleles should fix linked recessive deleterious mutations with a higher probability than recessive S-alleles (Llaurens et al., 2009b), but in natural populations we observed no difference in the total number of putatively deleterious linked to dominant vs. recessive S-alleles. To clarify this discrepancy, we took advantage of our sequencing of multiple copies of S-alleles to consider separately the fixed and the segregating mutations linked to each of the S-allele lineages. For each population, we included only mutations that were segregating and excluded those that were locally fixed. In agreement with the prediction of Llaurens et al., 2009b, we observed that lineages of dominant S-alleles do indeed tend to fix deleterious mutations more readily (Figure 4; Supplementary file 1f). This conclusion held true when extending the analysis to all non-synonymous mutations and to the lowly and the moderately deleterious mutations predicted by SNPeff (Supplementary file 1f). This was also true using SIFT4G to identify deleterious mutations, with the only exception of a nonsignificant correlation for A. halleri, which might be due to the low number of nucleotide sites included in the SIFT4G database, resulting in low power to detect differences (Supplementary file 1f). The fact that dominant S-alleles tend to fix deleterious mutations more readily but do not accumulate a larger total number of deleterious mutations is explained by the fact that the structure of the genetic load differs between dominant and recessive S-alleles: the dominant S-alleles tend to have more fixed deleterious mutations, but the recessive S-alleles compensate by accumulating a larger number of segregating mutations, resulting in similar numbers of deleterious mutations overall in most of the populations. ![Figure 4.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/94972/elife-94972-fig4-v1.jpg) **Figure 4.:** Each dot represents the value obtained for haplotypes linked to one S-allele in one population. An outside expert evaluated your responses to the original reviewers and offered the following comments:

The main criticism was whether deleterious variants were appropriately classified in the work. The authors use two different methods to characterize the effect of alleles to satisfy these comments. The result is somewhat complex. The authors do replicate the effect of dominance on fixation and segregation of deleterious alleles by classifying polymorphisms as synonymous or synonymous with SNPeff. This is not entirely surprising as it is approximately equivalent to classifying based on fold degeneracy (but it includes sites that have other than 0 or 4 fold degeneracy). However, the authors do not mention in the text that their observation of increased segregating deleterious mutations in recessive alleles was only statistically significant in A. halleri (for both analyses). Using SIFT, the authors only find an effect of dominance in A. lyrata. So in reality, while the trends are the same across the analyses, the statistical significance of the effects of dominance was not consistent.

Reviewer 2 had several more detailed criticisms of the manuscript. The first was that the authors should explore the dominance of linked deleterious mutations themselves. I agree that this would be interesting, but it is very difficult to accomplish, and I agree with the author's reluctance to do much more here. The reviewer also criticized the authors simulation approach. The authors provided their simulation script as requested, but declined to do additional simulations under varied selection coefficients. I felt this was a minimally adequate response to the reviewers concerns, but the authors could have reasonably conducted a few additional simulations under varied selection coefficients.

I think that the scope of the findings described in the assessment was reasonable. This is interesting work, but despite the author's arguments, the system is somewhat unique if for no other reason than that balancing selection at S-loci is uniquely strong

results.result: The manuscript establishes the theoretical and empirical background for studying the S-locus system in Arabidopsis. Long-term balancing selection on self-incompatibility alleles is expected to lead to accumulation of deleterious mutations in linked regions. The S-locus in Brassicaceae is controlled by a single non-recombining region, with S-alleles organized into four dominance classes controlled by small RNAs. Recessive S-alleles reach higher frequencies and can form homozygotes more often than dominant alleles.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C10 are well-supported by citations to established theoretical and empirical work in population genetics and plant reproductive biology. These claims provide the foundational knowledge for the study and are appropriately referenced to prior literature.

results.result: The authors successfully sequenced and phased 126 distinct S-allele copies across five populations (two A. halleri and three A. lyrata), reconstructing 34 haplotypes in Nivelle, 38 in Mortagne, and 16, 22, and 16 in IND, PIN, and TSS respectively. Nine S-alleles were shared between the two A. halleri populations. The phased sequences comprised 4,854 variable sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19 and C62 describe the sequencing and phasing results, which are directly supported by the Materials and methods section and Supplementary file 1e. The sample sizes and numbers of reconstructed haplotypes are clearly stated and represent substantial empirical data.

results.result: Linkage to the S-locus distorts phylogenies over approximately 10-30 kb along the chromosome. The phylogenetic structure shifts from clustering by S-alleles near the S-locus to clustering by populations at greater distances. FST analyses confirm high differentiation among S-alleles close to the S-locus that decays with distance, while population differentiation shows the opposite pattern. Each S-allele is associated with unique SNPs within 50 kb, and the same suite of mutations is consistently associated with copies of a given S-allele within populations. This association is lost at greater distances and when comparing across populations, suggesting recombination decouples alleles from linked sites faster than migration homogenizes genetic composition.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C20-C26, C39-C42, C63-C65 are strongly supported by multiple complementary analyses presented in Figure 2 and related supplements, including phylogenetic likelihood comparisons, FST analyses, MCA, and association studies. The convergence of multiple analytical approaches strengthens these conclusions about the spatial extent and population structure of linkage disequilibrium around the S-locus.

results.result: Phenotypic experiments with 399 offspring from six crosses revealed a significant decrease in Ah03/Ah03 homozygotes at the reproductive stage compared to Mendelian expectations, while Ah01/Ah01 and Ah04/Ah04 homozygotes showed normal survival. The increased mortality was associated with Ah03 homozygosity specifically, not with carrying the Ah03 allele itself (as heterozygotes showed normal proportions). A genetic load was thus detected linked to Ah03, an S-allele at intermediate dominance level.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13, C56-C60 are supported by experimental data in Table 1 and statistical tests showing departures from Mendelian ratios. The experimental design using dominance interactions to create homozygotes (rather than CO2 treatment) is clearly described. However, the sample size is modest and limited to three S-alleles, which the authors acknowledge.

results.result: Phenotypic measurements of 13 traits showed no overall effect of S-locus homozygosity except for maximum flowering stem length (opposite to expectation) and no effect of S-allele dominance except for time to first leaf (also opposite to expectation). The magnitude of S-linked load varied among S-alleles, with some showing detectable effects and others not. The results did not replicate the previous observation by Llaurens et al. 2009b that dominant S-alleles carry more severe load than recessive S-alleles.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15, C38, C61 are supported by phenotypic data in Figure 1 and Supplementary files, with appropriate statistical analyses (permutations and GLMs). The failure to replicate prior findings is honestly reported. The authors acknowledge limitations including modest sample sizes and the restriction to intermediate dominance levels. The observation that detected effects were opposite to expectations raises questions but is appropriately reported.

results.result: Genomic analyses found no overall effect of S-allele dominance on the total number of zerofold degenerate mutations (S0f) or the S0f/S4f ratio in either A. halleri (p=0.54) or A. lyrata (p=0.07). This conclusion held when extending analyses to all non-synonymous mutations or to deleterious mutations predicted by SIFT4G and SNPeff.
results.evaluation: Claims C27 and C66 are supported by GLM analyses presented in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1f. Multiple methods for identifying deleterious mutations converge on the same conclusion. The statistical tests are appropriate, though the p-value of 0.07 for A. lyrata approaches significance and might warrant discussion of borderline effects.

results.result: Dominant S-alleles tend to fix linked deleterious mutations more readily than recessive S-alleles. This pattern was observed in genomic data and held true when extending analyses to all non-synonymous mutations and to lowly and moderately deleterious mutations predicted by SNPeff.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C28, C67 are supported by genomic analyses in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 1f showing significant correlations between dominance and fixed deleterious mutations. The robustness across multiple definitions of deleterious mutations strengthens the conclusion. This represents a key empirical finding that partially supports theoretical predictions.

results.result: Recessive S-alleles accumulate more segregating (non-fixed) deleterious mutations compared to dominant S-alleles. Many deleterious mutations linked to recessive S-alleles are segregating rather than fixed.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C54 are supported by genomic data in Figure 4 showing the inverse relationship between dominance and segregating mutations. This finding complements the observation about fixed mutations and is critical to the overall conclusion about load structure.

results.result: The structure rather than the overall magnitude of the linked genetic load differs between dominant and recessive S-alleles. Dominant S-alleles have more fixed deleterious mutations while recessive S-alleles have more segregating mutations, resulting in similar total numbers of deleterious mutations overall. The dominance level of S-alleles modifies the structure of the genetic load they shelter.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C29, C69 represent the central conclusion integrating results from Figures 3 and 4. The logic is sound: no difference in total load (Figure 3) combined with opposite patterns for fixed vs. segregating mutations (Figure 4) implies structural differences. This synthesis is well-supported by the data and represents a novel insight.

results.result: Stochastic simulations confirmed that dominant S-alleles accumulate more fixed deleterious mutations while recessive S-alleles accumulate more segregating mutations, with the mean total number of mutations per S-allele copy remaining similar across dominance levels. These simulation predictions align with the genomic observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32, C68 are supported by simulation results in Figure 5. The simulations provide theoretical support for the empirical genomic findings. However, the authors acknowledge limitations: simulations assume fully recessive deleterious mutations and do not incorporate recombination between S-alleles and linked sites. These simplifications may affect quantitative predictions but the qualitative patterns appear robust.

results.result: The dominant allele Ah15, previously associated with reduced fitness in homozygotes by Llaurens et al. 2009b, is one of the most 'loaded' alleles among dominant S-alleles in the Nivelle population based on genomic analysis.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 is supported by genomic data in Figure 3A showing Ah15 has an unusually high number of mutations. This observation helps reconcile the current study's failure to find a general dominance effect with the previous study's positive result, suggesting Ah15 may be an outlier.

results.result: The A. lyrata populations colonized North America from European ancestors 20-30,000 years ago and are less diverse than the A. halleri populations studied, which colonized northern France from German populations during the last century.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by appropriate citations to previous demographic studies. This background information helps interpret differences in patterns between species and populations.

results.result: S-locus homozygous genotypes formed by crossing individuals with identical alleles from different populations should reveal less load than crosses within populations, and the S-locus region could contribute to hybrid vigor.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are predictions/speculations based on the observation that linked mutations differ between populations. While the logic is reasonable, these remain untested hypotheses. The authors appropriately frame C36 as speculative ('could contribute'), but experimental validation would be needed to support these claims.

results.result: Across multiple studies, the most consistent pattern of sheltered load appears to be decreased juvenile survival, possibly because it is a highly integrative fitness measurement.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is an inference based on comparison across multiple cited studies. The reasoning is sound and appropriately qualified ('seems to be', 'possibly'), representing a reasonable synthesis of the literature.

results.result: Self-compatible intermediates required for new S-allele formation can self and form homozygotes. The differential load structure predicts that self-compatible mutants may segregate more readily for recessive than dominant S-alleles, leading to more efficient diversification dynamics for recessive S-allele lineages. This prediction aligns with the observation that the most dominant S-alleles show the deepest phylogenetic divergence in Arabidopsis.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 combine established knowledge (C44, C47 supported by citations) with new predictions (C45-C46) based on the current findings. While the logic connecting load structure to diversification dynamics is reasonable, these predictions remain untested. The alignment with phylogenetic patterns (C47) is suggestive but not definitive support. Further empirical work is needed.

results.result: In multiple systems under balancing selection (sex chromosomes, ruff supergene, Heliconius butterfly wing pattern supergene), haplotypes with greater genetic load also act genetically in a dominant manner, establishing a parallel with the S-locus observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are supported by appropriate citations to studies of other balanced polymorphism systems. The comparison is valid and helps place the S-locus findings in a broader evolutionary context. However, C51's claim that dominance is associated with greater load 'in all cases' may be overstated given the limited number of systems examined.

results.result: Previous theory showed that linked deleterious mutations favor evolution toward greater dominance rather than recessivity because S-alleles becoming recessive would form homozygotes and express their load. The observation that many deleterious mutations linked to recessive S-alleles are segregating suggests load expression will be less severe for recessive than dominant S-alleles, potentially decreasing the predicted asymmetry in dominance modifier evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53, C55 combine established theory (C52 supported by citation) with new insights from the current data. The reasoning in C55 is logical: segregating mutations in recessive alleles may remain masked even in homozygotes if different copies carry different mutations. This represents a novel theoretical insight, though formal modeling would strengthen the argument.

results.result: Phenotypic experiments crossing S-locus homozygotes and heterozygotes revealed genetic load linked to some S-alleles (particularly Ah03, an intermediate dominance allele) manifested as reduced survival, but failed to replicate the predicted pattern that dominant S-alleles carry more severe load than recessive S-alleles across multiple fitness traits.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not explicitly discuss the phenotypic experiments, but the editor's assessment notes the evidence is 'solid' while acknowledging that 'statistical significance varied between the two species.' The failure to replicate the dominance-load relationship and the limited detection of load effects across traits suggests the phenotypic evidence is weaker than the genomic findings.

results.result: Phylogenetic and population genetic analyses demonstrate that linkage to the S-locus distorts phylogenies and maintains associations with specific mutations within approximately 10-30 kb, with this association decaying with distance from the S-locus and differing between populations due to recombination occurring faster than migration can homogenize linked variation.
results.evaluation: The editor states 'the evidence supporting the findings is solid' and reviewers raised no concerns about these phylogenetic and linkage analyses. The characterization of the spatial extent of S-locus effects and population differences appears well-accepted.

results.result: Genomic analyses reveal that dominant S-alleles accumulate more fixed deleterious mutations while recessive S-alleles accumulate more segregating deleterious mutations, resulting in differences in the structure rather than overall magnitude of genetic load between dominance classes.
results.evaluation: The reviewer notes that 'the trends are the same across the analyses, the statistical significance of the effects of dominance was not consistent' between species and methods. Specifically, increased segregating mutations in recessive alleles was only significant in A. halleri, and using SIFT only showed dominance effects in A. lyrata. This inconsistency undermines confidence in the generality of the finding.

results.result: No overall effect of S-allele dominance on the total number of deleterious mutations (S0f or S0f/S4f ratio) was detected across multiple analytical approaches including zerofold degenerate sites, non-synonymous mutations, and predictions from SIFT4G and SNPeff.
results.evaluation: The reviewer acknowledges that 'the authors do replicate the effect' when 'classifying polymorphisms as synonymous or synonymous with SNPeff' and notes that extending analyses to multiple mutation classification methods 'led to identical conclusions' regarding lack of overall dominance effect on total load.

results.result: Stochastic simulations confirm that dominant S-alleles accumulate more fixed deleterious mutations while recessive S-alleles accumulate more segregating mutations, with these effects compensating such that total mutation load does not differ by dominance class, matching the genomic observations.
results.evaluation: The reviewer notes that the authors 'provided their simulation script as requested, but declined to do additional simulations under varied selection coefficients' and considers this 'a minimally adequate response.' The reviewer suggests 'the authors could have reasonably conducted a few additional simulations under varied selection coefficients,' indicating the simulation evidence is accepted but not fully convincing.

results.result: Large-scale sequencing and phasing of 126 S-allele haplotypes across five populations yielded 4854 variable sites, enabling reconstruction of haplotype structure linked to 12 distinct S-allele lineages in A. halleri and multiple lineages in A. lyrata populations.
results.evaluation: The editor describes this as 'valuable empirical work' with 'solid' evidence. No reviewer concerns were raised about the sequencing and phasing methodology or results.

results.result: The dominant allele Ah15, previously associated with reduced fitness, is confirmed to be one of the most 'loaded' alleles among dominant S-alleles in the Nivelle population based on genomic analysis.
results.evaluation: This finding reconciles previous phenotypic observations with genomic data and was not challenged by reviewers. It serves as validation of the genomic approach.

results.result: Background theoretical framework and established knowledge about balancing selection, S-locus genetics, dominance hierarchies, demographic history, and parallels with other genetic systems under balancing selection.
results.evaluation: These claims represent established knowledge from cited literature and theoretical background. The reviewer notes 'the system is somewhat unique if for no other reason than that balancing selection at S-loci is uniquely strong,' acknowledging the theoretical context while noting system-specific features.

results.result: Predictions about reduced load in inter-population crosses, potential contribution to hybrid vigor, differential segregation of self-compatible mutants, and implications for S-allele diversification dynamics based on the observed load structure.
results.evaluation: These are logical predictions and speculations based on the main findings. The editor notes 'it remains to be seen how generalisable the conclusions are beyond the specific system investigated here,' suggesting these predictions are accepted as reasonable inferences but require future testing.

results.result: Methodological details about the experimental design including sample sizes, crossing procedures, and genetic composition of offspring.
results.evaluation: These methodological claims were not challenged by reviewers and represent straightforward descriptions of experimental procedures.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on sequencing and phasing results (C16-C19, C62). Both evaluations find this evidence solid and well-supported, with no concerns raised about methodology or sample sizes.
Perfect agreement on total load analysis (C27, C66). Both find the GLM analyses showing no overall dominance effect on total load to be well-supported across multiple mutation classification methods.

Disagreement on simulation evidence (C30-C32, C68). OpenEval finds simulations supportive despite acknowledged limitations, while peer reviewer considers evidence 'minimally adequate' and suggests additional simulations under varied selection coefficients would strengthen conclusions.
Perfect agreement on Ah15 outlier finding (C43). Both evaluations accept this observation as valid and useful for reconciling current results with previous studies.

Strong agreement on phylogenetic and linkage analyses (C2, C20-C26, C39-C42, C65). Both find the multiple complementary approaches convincing for characterizing S-locus spatial extent and population structure, though peer review excludes C63-C64 from this grouping.

Significant disagreement on phenotypic experiments (C11-C13, C56-C60). OpenEval finds experimental data supported despite modest sample sizes, while peer reviewer rates evidence as UNCERTAIN, noting varied statistical significance between species and failure to replicate dominance-load relationship.

Disagreement on phenotypic load effects (C14-C15, C38, C61). OpenEval finds these claims supported with appropriate caveats, while peer reviewer considers evidence weaker due to inconsistent statistical significance and limited detection of load effects across traits.

Major disagreement on fixed deleterious mutations (C3, C28, C67). OpenEval finds this a well-supported key empirical finding, while peer reviewer rates as UNCERTAIN due to inconsistent statistical significance between species and methods.

Major disagreement on segregating mutations (C4, C54). OpenEval finds the inverse relationship well-supported and critical to conclusions, while peer reviewer notes this was only statistically significant in A. halleri, undermining confidence in generality.

Major disagreement on central conclusion about load structure (C5, C29, C69). OpenEval considers this synthesis well-supported and novel, while peer reviewer rates as UNCERTAIN due to inconsistent statistical significance of the underlying patterns.

Agreement on foundational theoretical claims (C1, C6-C10). Both accept these as established knowledge appropriately cited from prior literature, with peer reviewer acknowledging the unique strength of balancing selection at S-loci.
Agreement on demographic background (C33-C34). Both evaluations accept these as appropriately cited established knowledge from previous studies.

Disagreement on predictions about population differences (C35-C36). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are untested hypotheses requiring validation, while peer reviewer rates as SUPPORTED, accepting them as reasonable inferences requiring future testing.

Disagreement on diversification predictions (C44-C47). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting predictions remain untested despite reasonable logic, while peer reviewer rates as SUPPORTED, accepting them as logical predictions with acknowledgment that generalizability remains to be seen.

Both address C37 but with different groupings. OpenEval finds this inference well-supported as a synthesis of literature, while peer reviewer groups it with phenotypic experiments and considers the overall evidence UNCERTAIN.

Agreement on comparisons to other balanced polymorphism systems (C48-C51). Both accept these as appropriately cited, though OpenEval notes C51 may overstate the consistency of patterns across systems.

Agreement on theoretical insights about segregating mutations (C52-C53, C55). Both accept the established theory and novel reasoning, with OpenEval noting formal modeling would strengthen the argument and peer reviewer grouping these with established knowledge.

Both address methodological claims (C56-C59) but in different contexts. OpenEval groups these with phenotypic experiments and finds them supported, while peer reviewer treats them separately as straightforward procedural descriptions.
